Other Assessments and Duties

The Family Test may be considered alongside other assessments, such as the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) and the Child Rights Impact Assessment (CRIA).

If the policy is to impact children, then a CRIA should be completed to specify how and to set out mitigations. In the CRIA, policy makers should consider impacts on children’s rights as set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), an international agreement setting out comprehensive rights to everyone under the age of 18. The UK is bound by the UNCRC under international law but does not incorporate international treaties directly into domestic law. The UNCRC sets out that families, should be afforded necessary protection and that children should grow up in a family environment with an atmosphere of happiness, love and understanding.

Good Practice

Using family centred language (for example, ‘parents’ or ‘children’ rather than ‘households’ or ‘individuals’) can support clearer, more empathetic policymaking.

Publishing Family Test Assessments

Decisions on whether and how to publish Family Test assessments rest with individual departments, however transparency is encouraged. Publishing assessments, where appropriate, demonstrates consideration of both positive and negative impacts on families.

Family Test assessments may be requested through Parliamentary Questions or Freedom of Information (FOI) requests and should be handled in line with FOI legislation.

Help and Advice

DWP hosts a cross-government Family Test Network meeting to share learning, evidence and good practice.

For further information on the Family Test and how to apply this guidance or how to join the Family Test Network meeting, contact: family.test@dwp.gov.uk

Family Test Questions and Prompts

Question

What impact could the policy have on family relationships and all family members’ ability to engage in family life?

Prompt

A Family member can be defined by a wide range of relationships including but not limited to:

spouses: married couples, civil partners, partners

parents: biological, adoptive, guardians, foster parents, parents-in-law, grandparents, stepparents

children: children in care and kinship arrangements, adopted siblings, step-siblings, grandchildren, stepchildren, biological children

extended family members: uncles, aunts, cousins, siblings-in-law

Families should be examined in the context of intact, separated and blended families. The user should consider a wide range of familial relationships and their ability to interact with each other and build healthy relationships. This can be impacted by a family’s accessibility to resources such as:

green spaces for children and adults to utilise

transport to visit family members

social amenities e.g. museums, cinemas, arcades, sports clubs, music groups

internet connection and technology

employment rights e.g. flexible working hours and parental leave and pay

childcare

housing

energy supply

health and social care

Policymakers should also consider the roles of members of the family, with a particular focus on caring responsibilities. Caring responsibilities are not limited to adults and can include children-adult and children-children caring relationships such as older siblings with caring duties for younger family members as well as the role of young carers and non-dependent children. It is also important to consider how the policy could have an impact on the mental health and wellbeing of all family members as this can affect their ability to carry out their role and impact the quality of their relationships.

Question

How would the policy impact families going through key life events?

Prompt

It’s essential that policymakers look beyond ‘traditional’ family units or households when thinking about family impacts. Various circumstances could result in members of the family leaving the family or household or new family members joining.

Some examples of such circumstance could include but are not limited to:

moving away from family members (policymakers should take into consideration how the policy may affect family members who have moved away to a devolved nation)

those in education and moving from the family home e.g. school boarders and university students

deployment of a member of armed forces

pregnancy

children going into or leaving care/kinships/adoption/foster care

incarceration

bereavement

significant health diagnoses

These changes could impact the financial stability and emotional wellbeing of both the family member directly impacted and the rest of the family. Policymakers should also evaluate how the policy could support or hinder families from continuing to fulfil their responsibilities in the family structure.

Question

How would the policy impact families experiencing relationship breakdown and the process of reformation and/or rebuilding?

Prompt

Changes to the family structure can be a result of relationship breakdowns and partners taking the decision to separate or divorce. Individuals may also take the decision to form new relationships and remarry. Both changes in circumstance can impact an individual’s caring and financial responsibilities or obligations.

Some of the leading causes of relationship breakdown include:

financial problems

substance misuse

abuse

conflict

However, these themes can be present in all relationships. Policymakers should consider victims and survivors of domestic abuse in policymaking and should assess how their policy may impact their ability to leave an abusive relationship and continue to support their dependants.

Policymakers should also consider how policies will financially impact a family going through changes in structure.
